newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: U.S. Jews hail Swiss bank whistle-blower as hero.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Jews hail Swiss bank whistle-blower as hero.

text.p: A night watchman who blew the whistle on a Swiss bank's shredding of old documents amid the search for Holocaust accounts was hailed as a hero on Friday by U.S. Jewish leaders who held him up as a model for other Swiss.

"To us you are a hero," Anti-Defamation League (ADL) national director Abraham Foxman told now-unemployed bank guard Christoph Meili, presenting him a golden menorah and 50,000 Swiss francs ($36,100) to help cover living expenses and legal fees.

"You are not only a hero to us, the Jewish people, but to history. I believe you acted to save the honour of Switzerland," Foxman said after meeting top Swiss bankers to air his dismay over Union Bank of Switzerland's embarrassing slip-up.
Foxman said Meili's deed set an example of moral courage that had few precedents in Switzerland.

"What this country needs is the will and ability...to take a quantum moral leap to face the past," he said. There should be no retreat into a legalistic approach, offering compensation if a panel of historians produced proof of Swiss wrongdoing.

UBS says the destruction this month of old records from a subsidiary it acquired in 1945 was a "regrettable accident" and insists no client records were lost that could assist the search for any dormant wealth of Holocaust victims in Swiss banks.

Meili smuggled bank documents out of UBS headquarters and gave them to Zurich Jewish leaders, who alerted prosecutors. They are now investigating whether UBS broke a ban on destroying relevant records or if Meili violated Swiss banking secrecy.
Foxman, whose group aims to fight bigotry and anti-Semitism, chided the Swiss for debating whether Meili did the right thing.
"Maybe he did break the law to prevent a crime," he told reporters. "What crime? The crime of hiding the past."

He also called on other Swiss to come forward with any information they have that could help track down funds hidden in Swiss banks by Jews afraid of the Nazis. He suggested the government encourage them and grant them immunity for doing so.

"There are thousands of people, simple people, who during the years of the war were clerks, were secretaries, were messengers, were recorders. They know some of the truth that has been shredded in the past and has disappeared," he said.
"I would like to hear from the centre of power in Berne that it is an act of glory, it would be an act to save the honour of Switzerland, to stand up and volunteer their information."
Meili, 28, added his support to the idea.
"I would like to make an appeal that if there are people in Switzerland who know of these things, that they have the courage to do something so that light is shed on the subject," he said.

Foxman met six senior bankers -- including the chief executives of Credit Suisse Group and Swiss Bank Corp, UBS's top layer and officials from the Swiss Bankers Assocation -- for 90 minutes in Zurich's most luxurious hotel.

He urged them to take the lead in the growing public debate over Switzerland's role as a wartime financial centre that nurtured Nazi economic dependency as a way to maintain its own independence and democracy.

The debate includes a row over Jewish charges that Swiss banks are still hoarding Holocaust victims' huge wealth, and Switzerland's anti-Jewish wartime immigration policy turned back thousands of Jews to near-certain death.

"We challenged them to creatively address the issue, and in the hour and a half we found a greater sense of urgency, a greater sense of understanding, a greater sense of the need to deal with it than we found in any other sector," Foxman said. ($1=1.3852 Swiss Franc)
